passage: My name is Nirmala. Last term I lost the chess club game to Tenzin, and I was so angry that I called him a cheat and a show-off in front of everyone. I said the same things at lunch, and I stopped saying hello. I thought that if Tenzin was my enemy, losing would hurt less. It did not. Then Tenzin left a note on my desk: "Want a rematch on Friday? I will show you the opening I practise." I felt silly. The game was one thing, and Tenzin was another. On Friday we played again. I lost by a little, but for the first time I laughed.

qa.q: What did Nirmala call Tenzin after losing the chess game?
qa.a: Nirmala called him a cheat and a show-off in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala think of Tenzin as an enemy?
qa.a: Nirmala thought that if Tenzin was an enemy, losing would hurt less, so the taunts came from hurt pride, though the plan did not work.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do the next time Nirmala loses a game?
qa.a: Nirmala could notice the sting, say well played or ask about the winning idea, and keep the game separate from the person.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt when Nirmala taunted him?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and confused because he had only played chess, but his note suggests he still wanted to be friends. 🙂

grounding: Nirmala treats the winner as an enemy and taunts, then learns to separate the game from the person.
